candidates.stimulus_use: 'Reveal what is omitted', with 'counting', 'bookkeeping' and 'a year', suggested setting the prescription that services count beside the thing they often leave out: whether the medicine is still being taken 12 months later.
candidates.working_title: Counting the bone medicine at 12 months
candidates.core_insight: Many people who start an oral bone medicine after a fracture have stopped within a year, so a bone plan needs named checks at about 16 weeks and 52 weeks, not only a first prescription.
candidates.angle: Records and many service reports count the start of treatment. The international patient-level indicators for fracture liaison services add two checks that are easy to skip: a monitoring contact within 16 weeks and whether the person is still prescribed treatment at 52 weeks. Persistence with oral bisphosphonates in real-world studies varies from poor to good, which is the argument for counting it.
candidates.position: Every bone treatment plan after a fracture should include a named follow-up at about 16 weeks and at 52 weeks to find out whether the medicine is being taken, because a prescription on the record does not show this.
claims_needing_evidence: In real-world studies, the proportion of people still taking an oral bisphosphonate at one year ranged from about 18% to 75% (systematic review of 89 observational studies: Fatoye 2019, BMJ Open).

The IOF Capture the Fracture, NOF and FFN patient-level KPI set for fracture liaison services includes monitoring within 16 weeks of the sentinel fracture and being prescribed anti-osteoporosis medication 52 weeks after it (Javaid 2020, Osteoporos Int).
Poor adherence to bisphosphonates is associated with higher fracture rates in observational studies (meta-analysis, e.g. Imaz 2010); association, not proof of cause.

UK FLS-DB reports show how many services record the 16-week monitoring and 12-month indicators (RCP FLS-DB annual report; check completeness figures before any claim that 'fewer services count this').

candidates.stimulus_use: 'Find the first question worth asking' and 'translating' suggested the question that turns a bone density T-score into a decision.
candidates.working_title: After the scan, ask for the fracture risk
candidates.core_insight: A bone density T-score is one input: whether treatment is advised depends on your overall chance of breaking a bone, which also counts age, previous fractures, steroid tablets, family history and other factors.
candidates.angle: People leave a bone density scan with a word (osteopenia, osteoporosis) and a number. Most fragility fractures happen in people whose T-score is above the osteoporosis line, so the word on its own can falsely reassure or falsely alarm. The first useful question translates the scan into a chance of fracture and a decision.
candidates.position: After a bone density scan, ask what your chance of breaking a bone is and whether that means treatment, because the T-score alone does not decide it.
claims_needing_evidence: UK guidance bases treatment decisions on fracture probability (FRAX, with or without bone density), with intervention thresholds that depend on age, not on the T-score alone (NOGG 2022, Gregson, Arch Osteoporos).

In a cohort of 149,524 postmenopausal women, 82% of those who had a fracture in the next year had peripheral T-scores better than -2.5 (Siris 2004, Arch Intern Med; peripheral densitometry, so state the method).

FRAX inputs include age, sex, weight, height, previous fracture, parental hip fracture, smoking, glucocorticoids, rheumatoid arthritis, secondary osteoporosis, alcohol and femoral neck bone density (Kanis 2008, Osteoporos Int; FRAX tool).

candidates.gain: A question that turns a confusing number into a decision.

candidates.stimulus_use: 'Test a familiar slogan against the evidence' prompted testing the common advice that walking keeps your bones strong.
candidates.working_title: Walking and bone: testing a familiar piece of advice
candidates.core_insight: Walking helps heart, mood and balance, but trials of walking on its own found little effect on spine bone density; UK consensus advice for bone is resistance (strength) exercise and, where suitable, impact exercise, alongside walking.
candidates.angle: The correction adds to walking; it does not replace it. A meta-analysis found no significant change in spine bone density with walking programmes and an inconsistent small effect at the hip. The UK consensus recommends resistance and impact exercise for bone strength, adapted for people with spinal fractures.
candidates.position: For bone, advise strength exercise and suitable impact exercise in addition to walking; walking alone is a weak way to protect bone density.
claims_needing_evidence: A meta-analysis of eight walking trials in postmenopausal women found no significant change in lumbar spine bone density; effects at the femoral neck were inconsistent (Martyn-St James 2008, Bone).

The UK consensus statement recommends resistance and impact exercise to maximise bone strength, strength and balance activities to reduce falls, and says people with spinal fracture or multiple low-trauma fractures should usually limit impact to about the level of brisk walking (Brooke-Wavell 2022, BJSM).
Supervised high-intensity resistance and impact training improved bone density in postmenopausal women with low bone mass in a small randomised trial (LIFTMOR, Watson 2018, JBMR).

candidates.stimulus_use: 'Compare what is recorded with what is experienced' and 'the last week of life' suggested setting the medicine-list entry 'bone protection' beside the weekly routine it demands of someone near the end of life.
candidates.working_title: The weekly bone tablet in the last months of life
candidates.core_insight: In trials, bisphosphonates took about a year to prevent one non-spinal fracture per 100 women treated, so for someone likely to live only weeks or a few months, the tablet's routine may bring burden with little time to help, and stopping can be the right decision.
candidates.angle: The medicine list says 'alendronic acid weekly' and ticks a box. Taking it means an empty stomach, a full glass of water, half an hour upright, and often chalky calcium tablets twice a day. Near the end of life the time to benefit is longer than the time left. Denosumab is different: stopping it causes rapid bone loss, so it needs a planned decision if the person may live longer than several months.
candidates.position: When a person is likely to be in the last months of life, review bone medicines: oral bisphosphonates and calcium tablets can usually be stopped; denosumab needs a specific plan, not an unplanned stop, if the person may live for more than a few months.
claims_needing_evidence: In a meta-analysis of 10 trials in postmenopausal women with osteoporosis, 12.4 months of bisphosphonate treatment were needed to prevent one non-vertebral fracture per 100 women, and 20.3 months to prevent one hip fracture per 200 women (Deardorff 2022, JAMA Intern Med).

STOPPFrail (version 1, 2017, and version 2, 2021) lists osteoporosis drugs and calcium supplements among medicines to consider stopping in frail older people approaching end of life (Lavan 2017; Curtin 2021, Age Ageing; check the exact criteria wording).
Alendronic acid must be taken fasting, with a full glass of plain water, followed by 30 minutes upright before food or other medicines (SmPC).
After stopping denosumab, vertebral fracture rates rose to those of untreated people, and multiple vertebral fractures were more common (Cummings 2018, JBMR).

In a trial of one zoledronic acid infusion in 181 frail women in long-term care, fractures and deaths were not lower with treatment over 2 years (Greenspan 2015, JAMA Intern Med); useful as the result that complicates treatment in the frailest.

candidates.stimulus_use: 'Apply it to the poorest or most isolated person' turned the general autumn-and-winter vitamin D advice toward the person who rarely leaves the house.
candidates.working_title: Vitamin D all year for people who rarely go outside
candidates.core_insight: UK advice is that people who rarely get sunlight on their skin, including people who are housebound or live in care homes, should take 10 micrograms of vitamin D a day all year, not only in autumn and winter.
candidates.angle: The autumn-and-winter message reaches most people. The all-year message is for the people least likely to hear it: housebound people, care home residents, people who cover their skin outdoors, and people with dark skin. It is cheap and simple, and it depends on someone thinking to offer it.
candidates.position: Anyone who rarely gets outdoors should be offered a daily vitamin D supplement all year, and care homes and home care services should check that it is being taken.
claims_needing_evidence: UK advice: everyone should consider 10 micrograms of vitamin D a day in autumn and winter; people who are not often outdoors, live in care homes, or usually cover most of their skin outdoors should take it all year; people with dark skin may need it all year (SACN 2016; Public Health England 2016 advice; NHS vitamin D page).

NICE PH56 recommends increasing access to and use of vitamin D supplements in at-risk groups, including people aged 65 and over, people with little sun exposure such as those who are housebound or in care homes, and people with dark skin (NICE PH56, 2014, updated 2017).
From about October to March in the UK, sunlight does not contain enough UVB for the skin to make vitamin D (SACN 2016).

candidates.stimulus_use: 'Ask who bears the cost' suggested comparing the three common forms of bone medicine by where the effort and the risks fall.
candidates.working_title: Tablet, injection or drip: where the effort falls
candidates.core_insight: The main bone medicines put the effort in different places: the weekly tablet needs a strict morning routine from the person; the six-monthly injection needs a schedule that must not lapse; the yearly drip needs a hospital or clinic visit and often brings a short flu-like reaction after the first dose.
candidates.angle: Choosing a bone medicine is usually presented as a choice of drug. For the person, it is a choice of burden: who has to do what, how often, and what happens if it goes wrong. Naming this helps people choose the form they can keep up.
candidates.position: The form of bone medicine should be chosen with the person according to what they can manage and keep up, because each form puts its burdens in a different place.
claims_needing_evidence: Alendronic acid is taken once a week, fasting, with a full glass of plain water, followed by 30 minutes upright before food, drink or other medicines (SmPC).

Denosumab 60 mg is given by injection every 6 months; stopping or delaying it without switching to another treatment leads to rapid bone loss and a higher risk of multiple spinal fractures (SmPC; MHRA Drug Safety Update 2020; Cummings 2018).

Zoledronic acid 5 mg is given by intravenous infusion once a year; after the first infusion, 42.4% had an acute-phase reaction compared with 11.7% with placebo, usually mild or moderate with a median duration of 3 days (Reid 2010, JCEM).
UK guidance offers intravenous zoledronic acid or denosumab when oral bisphosphonates are unsuitable (NOGG 2022).

candidates.stimulus_use: 'Follow the event over time', 'handovers' and 'a year' suggested following one six-monthly injection schedule through a year of moves between hospital, care home and GP.
candidates.working_title: The bone injection that must not be forgotten
candidates.core_insight: Denosumab must be given every six months, and stopping or delaying it without a plan can cause rapid bone loss and several spinal fractures at once, so the next due date needs a named owner through every move between services.
candidates.angle: Following one illustrative year shows how the due date can fall between records: an injection in the GP surgery, an admission, a move to a care home, a new GP. Nobody decides to stop; the date passes. The practical protection is two questions any family can ask.
candidates.position: Anyone on denosumab, and their family, should know the date of the next injection and who is booking it, and denosumab should never be stopped without a plan to switch to another medicine.
claims_needing_evidence: Denosumab 60 mg (Prolia) is given every 6 months (SmPC).

After stopping denosumab, the vertebral fracture rate rose from 1.2 to 7.1 per 100 participant-years, and among those with a vertebral fracture after stopping, 60.7% had multiple fractures compared with 38.7% after stopping placebo (Cummings 2018, JBMR, post hoc analysis of FREEDOM).

In UK primary care data, delaying the next denosumab dose by more than 16 weeks was associated with a higher risk of vertebral fracture than on-time dosing (Lyu 2020, Ann Intern Med; observational, target trial emulation).
Guidance recommends switching to a bisphosphonate when denosumab is stopped (ECTS position statement, Tsourdi 2017 and 2021; NOGG 2022; MHRA 2020).

candidates.stimulus_use: 'Count something nobody counts' suggested counting what the fracture calculator records only as yes or no, or not at all: how many fractures, how recent, and how many falls.
candidates.working_title: FRAX asks yes or no. Count the fractures and the falls.
candidates.core_insight: FRAX records a previous fracture as yes or no and does not include falls, so a recent fracture, several fractures or frequent falls mean the calculated risk may be too low, and UK guidance lists these as reasons to adjust the decision.
candidates.angle: The calculator is a good start and a common shortcut. In older people the things it counts crudely (number and recency of fractures) or ignores (falls) are often what drives the next fracture. Counting them takes one line of history.
candidates.position: When using FRAX in an older person, record how many fractures, when they happened and how often the person falls, and adjust the treatment decision when these are present.
claims_needing_evidence: FRAX treats prior fracture as a single yes or no input (Kanis 2008; FRAX tool documentation).
FRAX does not include falls history as an input (Masud 2011, J Clin Densitom, official positions on falls and frailty in FRAX).
Fracture risk is highest in the first one to two years after a fracture, and published adjustments to FRAX account for recency (Kanis 2020, Osteoporos Int).
NOGG 2022 lists situations in which FRAX may underestimate risk, including recent fracture, multiple fractures, high-dose glucocorticoids and frequent falls (check exact list).
A previous fracture is associated with about a doubling of later fracture risk (Kanis 2004, Bone, meta-analysis).

candidates.stimulus_use: The speech and language therapist viewpoint, 'compare what is recorded with what is experienced' and 'the moment of discharge' suggested setting a swallowing assessment beside the bone tablet on the same discharge letter.
candidates.working_title: Check the swallow before the weekly bone tablet
candidates.core_insight: Oral bisphosphonates must be swallowed whole with a full glass of water and followed by 30 minutes upright, so for people who are unable to swallow tablets safely, have oesophageal problems or are unable to sit upright, a yearly infusion or six-monthly injection is usually the better choice.
candidates.angle: The swallowing assessment and the medicine list are written by different people and are rarely read side by side. A person whose medicines are crushed, or who has a modified diet, may still go home on weekly alendronic acid. The tablet then either irritates the oesophagus or is not taken properly.
candidates.position: Before prescribing or continuing an oral bisphosphonate, check swallowing, whether medicines are crushed and whether the person can stay upright for 30 minutes; if any of these fail, choose another route.
claims_needing_evidence: Alendronic acid is contraindicated in abnormalities of the oesophagus that delay emptying (such as stricture or achalasia) and in people unable to stand or sit upright for at least 30 minutes (SmPC).
Alendronic acid tablets should be swallowed whole and not chewed, crushed or allowed to dissolve in the mouth, because of the risk of oropharyngeal ulceration (SmPC).
Oesophagitis and oesophageal erosions have been reported with alendronate, particularly when dosing instructions were not followed (de Groen 1996, NEJM).
UK guidance offers intravenous zoledronic acid or subcutaneous denosumab when oral bisphosphonates are contraindicated or the person is unable to follow the dosing instructions (NOGG 2022).

candidates.stimulus_use: 'Reverse the default assumption' and 'margins' suggested reversing the idea that someone is too old to benefit, by looking at absolute risk.
candidates.working_title: Older age can raise the benefit of bone treatment
candidates.core_insight: Fracture risk rises steeply with age, so the same relative effect of a bone medicine prevents more fractures per 100 people treated in an older person with osteoporosis, provided they are likely to live longer than the time the medicine takes to help.
candidates.angle: 'At 88, is there any point?' is a common default. The arithmetic of absolute risk runs the other way when osteoporosis is confirmed or a fracture has already happened. The limits are real and should be stated: in the HIP trial, women aged 80 and over selected mainly on non-skeletal risk factors showed no clear reduction in hip fractures, and the time to benefit is about a year.
candidates.position: Advanced age alone is a reason to assess fracture risk and often to treat, not a reason to withhold treatment; the limits are a likely survival shorter than the time to benefit, the absence of confirmed bone fragility, and the person's own goals.
claims_needing_evidence: Ten-year fracture probability rises steeply with age at any given bone density (FRAX; Kanis 2008).

Absolute benefit equals baseline risk multiplied by the relative risk reduction, so a similar relative effect gives a larger absolute effect at higher baseline risk (arithmetic; state as illustration).

In the HIP trial, risedronate reduced hip fracture in women aged 70 to 79 with confirmed osteoporosis (1.9% versus 3.2%) but did not show a clear reduction in women aged 80 and over selected mainly on non-skeletal risk factors (4.2% versus 5.1%, P=0.35) (McClung 2001, NEJM).
Time to benefit for bisphosphonates was about 12 months to prevent one non-vertebral fracture per 100 women (Deardorff 2022).

Analyses of trials in women aged 75 or 80 and over found fracture reductions with zoledronic acid or risedronate (e.g. Boonen 2010, J Am Geriatr Soc; Boonen 2004, J Am Geriatr Soc) (unsure; check before use).

candidates.core_insight: In a trial of 2,000 women aged 65 and over with osteopenia, four zoledronate infusions 18 months apart reduced fragility fractures over six years, with 15 women treated to prevent one woman having a fracture; that trade-off deserves an open conversation.

The trial gives a specific, discussable trade-off: four infusions, possible flu-like reactions, 15 treated for one fracture avoided. Many women in the trial had a low 10-year hip fracture risk, so it does not mean everyone with osteopenia should be treated.
candidates.position: An osteopenia result should start a conversation about fracture risk and options; for some older women at higher risk, zoledronate is a reasonable choice after the numbers are discussed openly.

Median 10-year hip fracture risk at baseline in that trial was 2.3% (Reid 2018).
UK treatment decisions depend on FRAX-based thresholds rather than on the T-score category (NOGG 2022).
Acute-phase reactions are common after a first zoledronate infusion (Reid 2010).

candidates.angle: People leave an appointment reassured and are not told what should bring them back. Asking the question at the time turns a one-off verdict into a plan with triggers.
candidates.position: When told you do not need bone treatment yet, ask what would change that, write the answer down, and go back if one of those things happens.

Taking oral glucocorticoids for 3 months or more increases fracture risk, and UK guidance advises fracture risk assessment for people starting or taking them (NOGG 2022 glucocorticoid section).
Height loss of 4 cm or more, or new back pain with risk factors, is a reason to consider spinal imaging for vertebral fracture (NOGG 2022; check exact thresholds).
A previous fracture is associated with about a doubling of later fracture risk (Kanis 2004, Bone).

candidates.stimulus_use: 'Look at the smallest practical detail', the community pharmacist viewpoint and 'the first hour' suggested the first 30 minutes after taking alendronic acid.
candidates.working_title: The first half hour after the weekly bone tablet
candidates.core_insight: Alendronic acid is absorbed in tiny amounts, and coffee, juice, food or other tablets taken too soon cut that further, so take it first thing with a full glass of plain water, stay upright, and wait at least 30 minutes before breakfast, drinks or other medicines.
candidates.angle: The leaflet's rules look fussy. Each has a reason: absorption is under 1% even when taken correctly; coffee or orange juice reduced it by about 60% in a pharmacokinetic study; lying down raises the chance of the tablet irritating the gullet. A pharmacist can go through the routine in two minutes.
candidates.position: explanatory, no position
claims_needing_evidence: Oral bioavailability of alendronate averaged 0.76% when taken fasting with water; black coffee or orange juice taken with it reduced bioavailability by about 60%; taking it with or after breakfast reduced it by more than 85% (Gertz 1995, Clin Pharmacol Ther).

Alendronic acid should be taken after getting up, with a full glass of plain water (at least 200 mL), at least 30 minutes before the first food, drink or other medicine; the person should not lie down for at least 30 minutes and until after the first food; not at bedtime; mineral water is unsuitable (SmPC).
If a weekly dose is missed, take one tablet the morning after remembering and return to the usual day; do not take two on one day (SmPC and patient leaflet; check wording).
Oesophagitis has been linked with alendronate, especially when instructions were not followed (de Groen 1996, NEJM).

candidates.working_title: Bisphosphonate drug holidays: who can pause, who should continue
candidates.core_insight: After about five years of an oral bisphosphonate or three years of yearly zoledronate, a review can offer a pause to people at lower risk, while people with a previous hip or spinal fracture, a fracture during treatment or high-dose steroids usually continue; denosumab has no holiday.
candidates.angle: 'Drug holiday' is used as if it applies to every bone drug and every person. It is a risk-based decision with a date to reassess. Bisphosphonates stay in bone and their effect wears off slowly; atypical femoral fracture risk falls quickly after stopping. Denosumab is the opposite and must be switched, not paused.
candidates.position: A bisphosphonate holiday should be a named, risk-based decision with a reassessment date, not an automatic stop at five years; denosumab should never be paused without switching to another treatment.
claims_needing_evidence: In FLEX, women who continued alendronate beyond 5 years had fewer clinical vertebral fractures than those who switched to placebo, with no difference in non-vertebral fractures (Black 2006, JAMA).
In the HORIZON extension, 6 versus 3 years of zoledronic acid reduced morphometric vertebral fractures, with no clear difference in other fractures (Black 2012, JBMR).

The ASBMR task force and NOGG 2022 recommend reassessment after 5 years of oral or 3 years of intravenous bisphosphonate, with continuation for people at high risk, such as those with previous hip or vertebral fracture, a fracture during treatment, or high-dose glucocorticoids (Adler 2016, JBMR; NOGG 2022; check the exact NOGG criteria including any age threshold).
Atypical femoral fracture risk rises with duration of bisphosphonate use and falls rapidly after stopping (Black 2020, NEJM).
Stopping denosumab leads to rapid bone loss and increased multiple vertebral fractures; switching to a bisphosphonate is recommended (Cummings 2018; ECTS 2017/2021).

candidates.working_title: The flu-like days after the first bone infusion
candidates.core_insight: After a first zoledronic acid infusion, about 4 in 10 people have a short flu-like reaction such as fever, aches or tiredness, usually mild and lasting about three days, and it is uncommon with later infusions.
candidates.angle: Side effects and their real frequency: this common, brief one is often not explained in advance, so people are alarmed, think the drug has harmed them, or decline the second dose. Knowing what to expect, and that it is mainly a first-dose effect, changes the experience.
candidates.position: People offered zoledronic acid should be told beforehand about the common, short-lived reaction after the first infusion and that later infusions usually cause much less.
claims_needing_evidence: In HORIZON-PFT (7,765 women), 42.4% of the zoledronic acid group had an acute-phase reaction after the first infusion compared with 11.7% with placebo; symptoms peaked within a day, median duration 3 days, mild or moderate in 90%, and rarely led to stopping treatment (Reid 2010, JCEM).
The frequency of acute-phase reactions fell with the second and third infusions (Reid 2010 full text or Black 2007, NEJM; figures to verify).
The product information advises adequate hydration before the infusion and says paracetamol or ibuprofen shortly afterwards may reduce symptoms (Aclasta SmPC; check wording).

candidates.working_title: New thigh ache on a long-term bisphosphonate: X-ray both femurs
candidates.core_insight: Atypical femoral fractures are rare, but they are stress fractures that can give weeks of aching thigh or groin pain beforehand and can occur on both sides, so new thigh pain in someone on long-term bisphosphonate or denosumab needs full-length X-rays of both femurs.
candidates.angle: Posts about this harm usually stop at 'rare'. The practical point is that the warning pain gives a chance to find an incomplete fracture before it completes. Absolute risk is low and rises with duration; it falls after stopping.
candidates.position: Ask about thigh and groin pain at every review of long-term bisphosphonate or denosumab, and arrange full-length X-rays of both femurs if it is present.
claims_needing_evidence: Atypical femoral fractures are stress or insufficiency fractures of the subtrochanteric region or femoral shaft; absolute risk on bisphosphonates ranges from 3.2 to 50 per 100,000 person-years, possibly around 100 per 100,000 with long-term use (Shane 2014, ASBMR task force).
Prodromal thigh or groin pain and bilateral fractures are common features (Shane 2014 full text; check the proportions).

Risk rises with duration of bisphosphonate use, falls rapidly after stopping, and is higher in Asian women; after 3 years of treatment in White women, 149 hip fractures were prevented for 2 atypical fractures (Black 2020, NEJM).
Atypical femoral fractures have also been reported with denosumab (Shane 2014; Prolia SmPC).
MHRA advice asks prescribers to evaluate thigh, hip or groin pain in patients on bisphosphonates for incomplete femoral fracture (MHRA Drug Safety Update 2011; unsure date).

candidates.working_title: Cement for spinal fractures: what sham-controlled trials found
candidates.core_insight: When vertebroplasty (injecting cement into a fractured vertebra) was compared with a sham procedure, pain and function improved about as much in both groups, and open trials against usual care probably overestimated the benefit.
candidates.angle: An intervention whose benefit is commonly misunderstood. Pain from a spinal fracture often improves over weeks, and people who have a procedure expect to feel better; a sham comparison separates the two. One trial in people with very recent fractures in hospital reported benefit, which keeps the question open for a narrow group.
candidates.position: Vertebroplasty should not be offered as routine treatment for painful osteoporotic spinal fractures; good pain relief, gradual return to activity, physiotherapy and treatment of the osteoporosis come first.
claims_needing_evidence: A Cochrane review of 21 trials found high- to moderate-quality evidence from five placebo-controlled trials that vertebroplasty gives no clinically important benefit for pain, disability or quality of life at one month compared with a sham procedure (Buchbinder 2018).
The review's sensitivity analyses indicated that open trials against usual care probably overestimated benefit (Buchbinder 2018).
Serious adverse events including osteomyelitis and cord compression have been reported after vertebroplasty (Buchbinder 2018).
One sham-controlled trial in inpatients with fractures under 6 weeks old reported greater pain reduction with vertebroplasty (Clark 2016, Lancet, VAPOUR).

NICE TA279 (2013) recommends vertebroplasty only for severe ongoing pain after a recent, unhealed vertebral fracture despite optimal pain management, with the level confirmed by examination and imaging (check wording; official page may not open).

candidates.working_title: Replace 'be careful' with specific movement advice
candidates.core_insight: UK consensus advice for people with osteoporosis, including after spinal fractures, is to stay active with strength, balance and suitable impact exercise and to avoid postures with a lot of forward bending, which gives the person instructions instead of a worry.
candidates.angle: A common clinical shortcut: 'be careful, don't lift anything'. Vague caution tends to mean less movement, weaker muscles and more falls. The consensus statement gives graded advice: most people can do resistance and impact exercise; people with spinal fracture or several low-trauma fractures usually keep impact to about the level of brisk walking and should get specialist advice.
candidates.position: Advice to people with osteoporosis should be specific and should encourage exercise; a general warning to be careful is insufficient and may lead to harmful inactivity.
claims_needing_evidence: The UK consensus recommends resistance and impact exercise for bone strength, strength and balance training to reduce falls, and spinal extension exercise for posture (Brooke-Wavell 2022, BJSM).

People with vertebral fracture or multiple low-trauma fractures should usually exercise only up to an impact equivalent to brisk walking (Brooke-Wavell 2022).
The statement says there is little evidence that physical activity causes significant harm and that benefits generally outweigh risks (Brooke-Wavell 2022).

candidates.working_title: Count the calcium you eat before adding a tablet
candidates.core_insight: Many people get enough calcium from food; UK guidance prefers calcium from diet and suggests supplements mainly when dietary intake is low, so it is worth estimating your daily intake before taking or refusing a calcium tablet.
candidates.angle: Calcium tablets are often added by default. They are large, can cause constipation and bloating, and some people stop their bone medicine because of them. Food first, with a supplement to make up a real shortfall, especially for people on bone medicines, who do need enough calcium and vitamin D.
candidates.position: Estimate dietary calcium before prescribing or buying calcium supplements, and use supplements to make up a shortfall rather than by default.
claims_needing_evidence: UK guidance recommends an adequate calcium intake (at least 700 mg a day for adults; check NOGG 2022 range for older people at risk), preferably from diet, with supplements if intake is low (NOGG 2022).
Dietary calcium intake was not associated with fracture risk in cohort studies, and the evidence that calcium supplements prevent fractures is weak and inconsistent (Bolland 2015, BMJ).
In the Women's Health Initiative, calcium plus vitamin D supplements increased kidney stones (Jackson 2006, NEJM).
People starting antiresorptive treatment should be calcium and vitamin D replete (SmPCs; NOGG 2022).
A free online calcium intake calculator is available from the University of Edinburgh (check it still exists and its current address; avoid implying any link with Alasdair).

candidates.working_title: The vitamin D trials that found no fracture benefit studied people who had enough
candidates.core_insight: Large recent trials found vitamin D supplements did not reduce fractures in generally healthy older adults who were mostly not deficient, which says little about people who are deficient, housebound or in care homes, or about vitamin D given alongside bone medicines.
candidates.angle: Keep a trial population separate from the people a claim is about. VITAL enrolled people not selected for deficiency or low bone mass; D-Health enrolled a general Australian population aged 60 to 84. An older trial in French care home residents with calcium and vitamin D reduced hip fractures. 'No benefit in people who have enough' and 'no benefit for anyone' are different findings.
candidates.position: Read the large null vitamin D trials as showing that extra vitamin D does not prevent fractures in people who already have enough; they do not remove the case for vitamin D in deficiency, low sun exposure or alongside bone treatment.
claims_needing_evidence: VITAL: 25,871 adults (men 50 and over, women 55 and over) not selected for vitamin D deficiency, low bone mass or osteoporosis; 2,000 IU a day for a median 5.3 years had no significant effect on total, non-vertebral or hip fractures (LeBoff 2022, NEJM).
D-Health: 21,315 Australians aged 60 to 84; 60,000 IU monthly for up to 5 years did not reduce total fractures (HR 0.94) (Waterhouse 2023, Lancet Diabetes Endocrinol).
Chapuy 1992: calcium and vitamin D3 reduced hip fractures in older women living in nursing homes or apartment houses for older people (NEJM; check population description and figures).
Meta-analyses find vitamin D alone does not prevent fractures in community-dwelling adults (Bolland 2018, Lancet Diabetes Endocrinol; Avenell 2014, Cochrane).

candidates.working_title: Very large, infrequent vitamin D doses: more was not better
candidates.core_insight: In a randomised trial of older women, a single very large dose of vitamin D each year led to more falls and more fractures than placebo, so daily or weekly doses are the safer way to give vitamin D.
candidates.angle: Vitamin D is often treated as harmless, so one big dose looks convenient. The Sanders trial found the opposite for 500,000 units once a year, with the excess concentrated in the three months after the dose. The evidence on monthly doses is mixed: one small trial found more falls with 60,000 units a month, while D-Health found no increase in fractures.
candidates.position: Avoid very large single doses of vitamin D, such as a yearly bolus, in older people; give daily or weekly doses, including when correcting deficiency.
claims_needing_evidence: In 2,256 community-dwelling women aged 70 and over at high fracture risk, 500,000 IU of oral cholecalciferol once a year for 3 to 5 years increased falls (rate ratio 1.15) and fractures (rate ratio 1.26) compared with placebo; the excess in falls was greatest in the first 3 months after dosing (Sanders 2010, JAMA).
In 200 adults aged 70 and over with a prior fall, 60,000 IU monthly was associated with more falls than 24,000 IU monthly (Bischoff-Ferrari 2016, JAMA Intern Med; check figures).
In D-Health, 60,000 IU monthly did not increase fracture risk (Waterhouse 2023).

The UK National Osteoporosis Society guideline recommends loading regimens in divided doses followed by regular maintenance (Aspray 2014, Age Ageing; check whether it advises against single large doses).

candidates.working_title: Hormone treatment for prostate or breast cancer: ask about your bones
candidates.core_insight: Hormone treatment for prostate cancer (androgen deprivation therapy) and aromatase inhibitors for breast cancer speed up bone loss and are linked with more fractures, so a fracture risk check at the start of treatment is worth asking for.
candidates.angle: Cancer care rightly concentrates on the cancer. Bone loss from long-term hormone treatment is predictable and can be assessed early. This also reaches men, who rarely think of osteoporosis as their problem.
candidates.position: Anyone starting long-term androgen deprivation therapy or an aromatase inhibitor should ask for a fracture risk assessment at the start of treatment.
claims_needing_evidence: Among men with prostate cancer surviving at least 5 years, 19.4% of those who received androgen deprivation had a fracture compared with 12.6% of those who did not (Shahinian 2005, NEJM; observational).
Aromatase inhibitors increase bone loss and fracture risk in postmenopausal women with breast cancer (e.g. ATAC bone substudy, Eastell 2008; joint position statement, Hadji 2017, J Bone Oncol).
NICE guidance for prostate cancer (NG131) and early breast cancer (NG101) includes recommendations on fracture risk or bone density assessment for people on these treatments (check exact wording).
UK osteoporosis guidance lists androgen deprivation therapy and aromatase inhibitors as causes of secondary osteoporosis (NOGG 2022).

candidates.working_title: In older people, read the hip result before the spine result
candidates.core_insight: In older people, arthritic bony spurs in the spine (and collapsed vertebrae or calcium in the aorta) can raise the spine bone density reading, so a reassuring spine result with a lower hip result should be read with care and the hip usually relied on.
candidates.angle: A common shortcut: reading the lowest-sounding summary line of a DXA report without asking why spine and hip disagree. Spinal osteophytes affect most people over 60 and add to the measured spine density; a compressed, fractured vertebra can also read as denser.
candidates.position: When spine and hip DXA results disagree in an older person, base the decision on the hip result and look in the report for degenerative change or fractured vertebrae.
claims_needing_evidence: In 434 people aged 60 to 99, lumbar osteophytes affected 75% of men and 61% of women and explained a substantial share of variation in spine BMD; osteoporosis was present at the hip in 33% of women and 26% of men but at the spine in only 24% and 4% (Liu 1997, Osteoporos Int).
The authors concluded that diagnosis and fracture risk assessment in older people should be based on hip BMD unless spinal osteoarthritis has been excluded (Liu 1997).
ISCD official positions advise excluding vertebrae affected by structural change or artefact from the spine BMD analysis (ISCD Adult Official Positions 2019; check wording).
FRAX uses femoral neck BMD (Kanis 2008; FRAX documentation).

candidates.working_title: Denosumab in advanced kidney disease: plan for calcium
candidates.core_insight: Denosumab is often the option when kidney function rules out a bisphosphonate, but in people on dialysis severe low calcium in the first 12 weeks was common, so calcium, vitamin D and bone and mineral status need checking before, with calcium measured in the weeks after.
candidates.angle: A qualification of an earlier point. E094 rightly said low eGFR should not mean no bone treatment. In advanced chronic kidney disease the bone problem may also be something other than osteoporosis (chronic kidney disease mineral and bone disorder), and denosumab carries a specific calcium risk that US regulators added as a boxed warning.
candidates.position: In advanced chronic kidney disease, start denosumab only after checking and correcting calcium and vitamin D, assessing mineral and bone disorder with the kidney team, and arranging calcium checks in the first weeks.
claims_needing_evidence: In female dialysis-dependent Medicare patients aged 65 and over, the 12-week weighted cumulative incidence of severe hypocalcaemia was 41.1% with denosumab versus 2.0% with oral bisphosphonates (Bird 2024, JAMA; observational).
In January 2024 the US FDA added a boxed warning for severe hypocalcaemia with Prolia in patients with advanced chronic kidney disease (FDA Drug Safety Communication; check date).
The Prolia SmPC requires hypocalcaemia to be corrected before starting and recommends calcium monitoring in people at risk, including severe renal impairment (check wording).
Chronic kidney disease mineral and bone disorder is nearly universal in dialysis-dependent patients and complicates diagnosis and treatment of bone fragility (Bird 2024 background; KDIGO 2017).

candidates.working_title: For very high fracture risk, the order of treatment changes the result
candidates.core_insight: For people at very high fracture risk, such as those with recent or multiple spinal fractures, starting with a bone-building drug (teriparatide or romosozumab) and then an antiresorptive prevented more new spinal fractures than an antiresorptive alone in head-to-head trials.
candidates.angle: The default is to start an oral bisphosphonate and see. For the highest-risk group, trial evidence favours building bone first, and some sequences work less well (switching from denosumab to teriparatide led to bone loss at the hip). Early identification and referral are the practical steps.
candidates.position: People at very high fracture risk should be identified and referred for consideration of anabolic treatment first, instead of starting an oral bisphosphonate by default.
claims_needing_evidence: VERO: in 1,360 postmenopausal women with severe osteoporosis, new vertebral fractures at 24 months occurred in 5.4% with teriparatide versus 12.0% with risedronate (Kendler 2018, Lancet).

ARCH: 12 months of romosozumab followed by alendronate reduced new vertebral fractures at 24 months (6.2% versus 11.9%) compared with alendronate alone; serious cardiovascular adverse events were more frequent with romosozumab in year one (Saag 2017, NEJM).
Switching from denosumab to teriparatide led to progressive or transient bone loss at the hip (Leder 2015, Lancet, DATA-Switch).

NOGG 2022 defines very high risk (for example recent or multiple vertebral fractures, very low T-score, high-dose glucocorticoids) and recommends considering anabolic treatment first; NICE TA791 approves romosozumab after a major osteoporotic fracture within 24 months (check criteria).

candidates.working_title: Hip protectors in care homes: a small benefit when they are worn
candidates.core_insight: In care homes, hip protectors probably reduce hip fractures a little (about 11 fewer per 1,000 residents), make little or no difference for people living at home, and help only if they are comfortable enough to be worn.
candidates.angle: A trade-off to discuss openly: a small benefit against comfort, heat, dressing, toileting and dignity. Adherence has been poor in trials, which is a design and care problem as much as a resident problem. They are one option alongside bone treatment and falls assessment, not a substitute.
candidates.position: Care homes should offer hip protectors as a choice to residents at high risk of hip fracture, with attention to fit, comfort and continence care, and never in place of bone treatment or falls assessment.
claims_needing_evidence: Pooled data from 14 studies (11,808 participants) in nursing or residential care found moderate-quality evidence of a small reduction in hip fracture (RR 0.82; 11 fewer per 1,000) (Santesso 2014, Cochrane).
Five community trials (5,614 participants) showed little or no effect on hip fracture (RR 1.15) (Santesso 2014).
Hip protectors may slightly increase pelvic fractures (1 more per 1,000); adverse events such as skin irritation ranged from 0% to 5%; long-term adherence was poor (Santesso 2014).

candidates.working_title: Show fracture risk as people out of 100
candidates.core_insight: People understand bone treatment choices better when their risk with and without treatment is shown as people out of 100 over a stated time, with a picture; an osteoporosis decision aid built this way improved understanding in trials.
candidates.angle: Care that works, with what makes it work: absolute numbers, the same denominator, a stated time period and an icon array. In the Osteoporosis Choice trial, women given the decision aid were more likely to know their 10-year fracture risk and the risk reduction from treatment; it did not change how many started treatment, which is the honest finding.
candidates.position: When discussing bone treatment, show the person's risk with and without treatment as people out of 100 over a stated number of years, ideally with a decision aid.
claims_needing_evidence: In a randomised trial of 100 women, the Osteoporosis Choice decision aid (pictographic 10-year fracture risk and absolute risk reduction) made women more likely to correctly identify their fracture risk (49% versus 28%) and risk reduction with bisphosphonates (43% versus 16%), with no difference in treatment start (Montori 2011, Am J Med).
A second trial found the decision aid improved knowledge and engagement compared with FRAX results alone or usual care (LeBlanc 2015, PLoS One).
A systematic review found that natural frequencies, absolute risks and visual aids improve understanding of risk (Zipkin 2014, Ann Intern Med).
NICE has published a patient decision aid for bisphosphonates with icon arrays (check title, year and whether it is current).

candidates.working_title: Acid-reducing tablets and fractures: link versus trial
candidates.core_insight: Observational studies link long-term proton pump inhibitors (PPIs) with fractures, but in a large randomised trial of pantoprazole for about three years there was no significant difference in fractures, so bone health alone is a weak reason to stop a PPI that is needed.
candidates.angle: Association versus causation. People who take PPIs for years differ from people who do not (age, illness, other medicines), so an observational link can arise without the drug causing fractures. Stopping PPIs that have no ongoing reason is still right, for other reasons.
candidates.position: Stop PPIs that no longer have an indication on their own merits; do not stop a needed PPI solely to protect bone.
claims_needing_evidence: In the COMPASS trial, 17,598 participants were randomised to pantoprazole 40 mg or placebo with median follow-up 3.01 years; there was no statistically significant difference in safety outcomes, which included fractures, except enteric infections (Moayyedi 2019, Gastroenterology).
Observational meta-analyses report associations between PPI use and fractures (e.g. Yu 2011; Zhou 2016) (unsure citations).
The US FDA issued a 2010 safety communication on possible fracture risk with high-dose or long-term PPIs (check wording).

candidates.working_title: Bone density is a stand-in for fractures
candidates.core_insight: A treatment can raise bone density without preventing fractures, as sodium fluoride did in a 1990 trial, so fractures and the person's function, not the density number on a repeat scan, are the outcomes to count.
candidates.angle: What gets counted: the DXA number is routine and easy to compare; the outcomes patients value are fewer fractures, less pain, keeping height and staying independent. Fluoride raised spine density by about a third and led to more non-spinal fractures. For approved drugs, density changes do track fracture reduction across trials, but a small change on one person's repeat scan is a poor guide to whether their treatment is working.
candidates.position: Do not judge an approved bone medicine by a small change on one person's repeat scan; check that it is being taken and look for new fractures, and use repeat DXA for specific questions.
claims_needing_evidence: In 202 postmenopausal women with osteoporosis and vertebral fractures, sodium fluoride increased lumbar spine BMD by 35% compared with placebo, new vertebral fractures were similar (163 versus 136), and non-vertebral fractures were higher (72 versus 24) (Riggs 1990, NEJM).

Across trials of approved osteoporosis drugs, larger treatment-related increases in BMD are associated with larger fracture reductions (Black 2020 Lancet Diabetes Endocrinol; Bouxsein 2019 JBMR; FNIH-ASBMR SABRE) (unsure citations).
For antiresorptive drugs, the BMD change in an individual explains only part of the fracture reduction (Cummings 2002, Am J Med) (unsure).
Repeat DXA changes smaller than the least significant change are within measurement error (ISCD positions).

candidates.working_title: Which spinal fractures did the trial count?
candidates.core_insight: Headline reductions in spinal fractures in osteoporosis trials often count fractures found on scheduled X-rays, many never noticed by the person; the absolute numbers for painful spinal fractures and hip fractures are smaller and are what many people want to know.
candidates.angle: In FIT, alendronate cut X-ray-detected spinal fractures from 15.0% to 8.0% and clinically apparent spinal fractures from 5.0% to 2.3% over three years. Both are clinically relevant, because X-ray-detected fractures predict later fractures, but a person deciding on treatment deserves both sets of numbers.
candidates.position: When explaining a bone medicine's benefit, give absolute numbers for the fractures people feel (painful spinal, hip, wrist) alongside X-ray-detected spinal fractures.
claims_needing_evidence: In FIT (2,027 women with existing vertebral fractures, 36 months), new morphometric vertebral fractures occurred in 8.0% with alendronate versus 15.0% with placebo, and clinically apparent vertebral fractures in 2.3% versus 5.0% (Black 1996, Lancet).
In FREEDOM, new radiographic vertebral fractures were 2.3% with denosumab versus 7.2% with placebo over 3 years, and hip fractures 0.7% versus 1.2% (Cummings 2009, NEJM; check figures).
Only a minority of vertebral fractures come to clinical attention (Cooper 1992 and later work; check the source for any proportion quoted).
Morphometric vertebral fractures predict future fractures (e.g. Lindsay 2001, JAMA) (unsure).

candidates.working_title: Dementia and bone treatment
candidates.core_insight: People with dementia have more fractures and, in population studies, are less likely to receive osteoporosis treatment; the decision should rest on the same grounds as for anyone else: likely benefit within the person's expected time, their goals, and a form of treatment they can manage.
candidates.angle: Who gets left out. In a Swedish population study, people with dementia had more osteoporotic fractures but were about a third as likely to use osteoporosis drugs after adjustment. The tablet routine can be impossible with dementia, but a yearly infusion or six-monthly injection removes that barrier. Evidence in the frailest care home residents is uncertain (ZEST), which is a reason for an individual decision, not for exclusion by diagnosis.
candidates.position: A diagnosis of dementia is not by itself a reason to withhold bone treatment; decide on expected benefit within the person's likely time, their goals, and a form of treatment that suits them.
claims_needing_evidence: In 2,610 people aged 66 and over in Stockholm, 25% of people with dementia and 7% without had an osteoporotic fracture in the previous 4 years, yet people with dementia were less likely to use osteoporosis drugs after adjustment (OR 0.34) (Haasum 2012, Osteoporos Int).
Dementia is associated with higher hip fracture risk (meta-analyses of cohort studies; find a reliable one before use).
In ZEST, a single zoledronic acid infusion in 181 frail women in long-term care increased BMD, with no reduction in fractures or deaths over 2 years (Greenspan 2015, JAMA Intern Med).
Time to benefit for bisphosphonates is about 12 months (Deardorff 2022).
